title: Only one sense amp per 16 bitlines: bitline charge queue
idea: Self-imposed limit: one sense amp per 16 bitlines. After the wordline fires, each bitline holds its charge-shared signal on its own ~40 fF capacitance behind an isolation switch, and one offset-compensated sense amp resolves and writes back the 16 bitlines one after another in ~2 ns slots while the wordline stays open; the requested slice is resolved first and the rest are restored in the background.
why: Periphery (fact 7): the sense-amp stripe is ~15-20% of the die, and sharing cuts its area ~8-10x (die area -10-12%). The cost is a longer tRAS for full-row restore, which hides behind fine-grained access.

title: Two-device sense amp: Esaki tunnel-diode Goto pair latch
idea: Limit: a sense amp may contain only two devices. Use a series pair of Si/SiGe Esaki tunnel diodes (a 1960s Goto pair) whose N-shaped I-V gives the shared node two stable points; a clocked bias ramp drives the node through its unstable point, and the +/-50 mV bitline nudge decides which stable state it falls into within ~50 ps.
why: Periphery area and speed: 2 devices instead of the 6-10 in an offset-compensated latch, which could cut the SA stripe by ~3x. Matching depends on peak current rather than Vt, so random dopant mismatch matters less; decisions cost sub-fJ.

title: Frequency-division wordline decoding with resonant driver gates
idea: Limit: zero logic gates in the row decoder. Each wordline-driver group is gated by a tiny resonant element (BAW or varactor tank) tuned to a unique frequency pair; the bank broadcasts two tones on one shared line, and only the group resonant at both rectifies enough voltage to fire, so address-to-frequency replaces the NAND decode tree.
why: Removes multi-stage decoder trees and predecode buses (~8-10% of the die) and frees one routing metal. Feasibility hinges on resonator size versus pitch, so it applies at subarray-select granularity, not per wordline.

title: EUV-free decoder: coarse mesowires plus stochastic doping and lookup map
idea: Limit: no EUV or immersion patterning in decoder transistors. Borrowing nanowire-crossbar decoders, a few coarse i-line address wires cross the dense wordline ends, and graded implant or gate-oxide thickness gives each wordline a unique threshold code; a post-fab BIST pass maps logical rows to the physical codes that actually work and stores the map in a few kb.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): pitch-matched decoder/driver strips are among the hardest periphery patterns; using cheap i-line plus calibration could drop 1-2 critical masks and cut decoder area ~30%.

title: Half the capacitor: negative-capacitance HZO preamp restores sense margin
idea: Limit: storage capacitor cut to 2.5 fF, so the bitline signal falls to ~40 mV. Place a series HZO ferroelectric layer in the gate stack of the sense amp's input pair, tuned to the negative-capacitance regime, so the internal gate swing is stepped up 2-4x before the latch regenerates.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): half the Cs lets pillar AR fall from ~70:1 to ~35:1, with cheaper etch and deposition and better yield, ~15-25% cost/bit. Risk: NC hysteresis and speed.

title: Ground-precharge charge-transfer preamp triples bitline length
idea: Limit: no VDD/2 precharge or equalizer devices. Bitlines precharge to ground, and a charge-transfer transistor biased at its threshold pumps the cell's charge from the big bitline into a ~1 fF sense node, giving a voltage gain of about C_BL/C_SN (~10x) before a small latch.
why: Periphery: 3x longer bitlines (1,536 cells per BL) mean 3x fewer SA stripes (die -8-10%). An old trick revived for the long vertical bitlines of 3D DRAM (fact 2).

title: No matched analog pairs: delay-chain arbiter sense amps
idea: Limit: the sense amp must be synthesizable from standard digital cells. BL and BLB each set the supply of a short starved inverter chain, the cell's +/-dV becomes a ps-scale delay difference, and an SR-latch arbiter at the end decides; mismatch is trimmed by digitally tuned delay taps calibrated at power-up.
why: U.S. manufacturability and periphery cost: sense amps that port to any logic fab or node, with digital calibration replacing matched-pair area (SA area -30-40%).

title: Noise as resource: dithered majority-vote sensing with tiny comparators
idea: Limit: comparator offset (sigma ~20 mV) is bigger than the signal (~15 mV). Inject a calibrated random dither on the reference, fire a minimum-size, unmatched, non-loading comparator 7-15 times in ~3 ns, and count: the signal skews the probability of ones (stochastic resonance), so the majority recovers the bit, and only then does the restore driver fire.
why: Sense margin and periphery area: comparators 4x smaller, plus tolerance of smaller Cs or longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: Column-gated double-gate access: only requested 64 cells ever open
idea: Limit: never disturb a cell you did not ask for. Give each vertical-channel access transistor a back gate tied to a column-enable line running orthogonally to the wordline, so a cell connects only when wordline AND column-enable are high; only the 64-bit target slice charge-shares, and only its 64 sense amps fire and restore.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): ~5.9 pJ per useful bit could fall to ~0.3-0.5 pJ, sense energy -95%, and partial activations reduce row-hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: No column decoder: CCD-style shift-out of the latched row
idea: Limit: no column decoder and no global column-select lines. After sensing, the sense amps are linked by two pass transistors each into a dynamic shift register that clocks the row out serially toward taps placed every 256 bits at the bank edge, like a CCD image sensor; random column access becomes 'shift N from the nearest tap'.
why: Periphery (fact 7): column decoders plus CSL wiring take ~5-8% of the die and one metal layer; streaming readout suits AI tensor fetches.

title: Zero offset budget: floating-gate trimmed sense amps
idea: Limit: sense amp offset must be zero. Each SA's cross-coupled pair includes a small charge-trap trim transistor programmed once at wafer test, from an on-die BIST measurement, to null that SA's own Vt mismatch, recovering ~15-20 mV of margin.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): the recovered margin lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3 fF (AR 70 to 45), so capacitor etch and deposition get cheaper, ~10-15% cost/bit.

title: No charge pumps: neighbor-wordline bootstrap boosts selected wordline
idea: Limit: no VPP charge pumps on the die. Local wordline drivers self-boost: a precharged, deselected neighbor segment's capacitance is coupled through a MIM capacitor to kick the selected wordline from VDD to ~3 V (like NAND channel boosting), and the charge is recycled back into the neighbor when the row closes.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): deleting VPP pumps (~3-4% of the die, 30-40% conversion loss) cuts wordline energy ~30-40%.

title: Stepwise adiabatic charging of wordlines from on-die tank capacitors
idea: Limit: 4x less activation energy without lowering any voltage. Wordlines and bitline restore are charged in N steps from a bank of deep-trench tank capacitors held at intermediate voltages, then discharged back step by step into the same tanks, so dissipation scales ~1/N.
why: CV^2 floor (fact 10): with N=4, wordline and restore energy fall ~60-75% for ~1-2 ns of extra latency; the tanks reuse dead area under the pads.

title: Array wafer carries only cells: periphery from U.S. legacy fabs
idea: Limit: the EUV array wafer may hold only cells and sense amps. Global decoders, pumps, I/O, DLL, test logic and fuses go on a 28/40 nm wafer from under-used U.S. legacy fabs and are joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at ~1 um pitch.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7), capital (fact 4), U.S. manufacturability: ~30% more bits per EUV wafer, with the periphery built on depreciated tools.

title: Transistor-free predecoders: threshold-switch diode matrix in BEOL
idea: Limit: decoders may use zero front-end transistors. Build predecoders as a BEOL crossbar of ovonic threshold switches and resistors above the array; the address bits applied to its columns make only one row's series OTS chain exceed threshold and snap on, firing that local wordline driver.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~6-9% of decoder silicon moves into stacked BEOL, with no extra EUV layers.

title: Tungsten-free periphery: molybdenum contacts and plate-layer routing
idea: Limit: zero tungsten (China ~80% of supply). Replace W contacts and M0 in the periphery with ALD molybdenum or ruthenium, and reuse the capacitor top-plate film (TiN/doped SiGe) as an extra local routing layer for decoder and SA interconnect, deleting one W metal level.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint and cost: removes W supply risk, saves one metal and mask level (~2-3% wafer cost), and Mo's lower resistance at small CDs speeds wordline straps.

title: Bitline capped at 10 fF: segment amplifiers inside the array tier
idea: Limit: no bitline may exceed 10 fF. Every 32 cells, a 2-transistor local amplifier (gate on the local bitline, drain on a global bitline) is built in the same vertical-channel tier as the access transistors, turning charge sharing into current gain on a global line.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): with a 4x smaller C_BL, Cs can drop to ~1.5-2 fF (planar or low-AR capacitors), which unblocks the 3D DRAM capacitor (fact 2).

title: No global datalines: each subarray bonds straight to logic die
idea: Limit: no bank-level global I/O buses or secondary sense amps. Each subarray's SA stripe has its own local hybrid-bond pads (~0.5 um pitch, ~1e5 per die) that land directly on the logic or accelerator die, so data leaves through the shortest vertical wire.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): ~3-4 pJ/bit could fall below 0.5 pJ/bit, and global I/O area (~5% of the die) disappears.

title: Zero-leakage idle sensing: pre-biased NEMS cantilever latch
idea: Limit: idle sense amps must leak exactly zero. Each SA is a nano-electromechanical relay biased within ~30 mV of pull-in, so the bitline differential tips the beam toward the BL or BLB electrode; once in contact it latches mechanically, then releases on reset.
why: Idle power and refresh energy (fact 3) plus periphery leakage: zero off-current and an abrupt switch. Risk: contact wear over 1e15 cycles and ~ns mechanical delay.

title: Erasure-flagging sense amps: weak decisions marked, not guessed
idea: Limit: accept a raw bit error rate of 1e-4. A second, time-delayed sample in each SA flags bits that resolved slowly (small |dV|) as erasures, and a short per-burst erasure code corrects up to 4 flagged bits per 64 B with little overhead, since known-location errors cost half the parity.
why: Sense margin: tolerating 1e-4 lets Cs shrink ~30% or refresh intervals lengthen 2-4x (facts 1, 3), with soft information borrowed from NAND applied to DRAM.

title: Same capacitor, +58% bits: tri-level cells with stepped-reference sensing
idea: Limit: no new cell and no new litho, only periphery. Store three charge levels (0, 1/2, 1) and sense in two steps: first against a +1/3 reference, then against a -1/3 reference created by coupling a small trim capacitor, packing 3 bits into 2 cells.
why: Density and cost per bit: +58% bits from the same array, paid for by ~20% more SA area and tighter margins, so it works best paired with offset trimming.

title: No in-house analog team: open memory-periphery compiler for startups
idea: Limit: a new-memory startup gets zero analog designers. A CHIPS/DARPA-funded open-source periphery generator (sense amps, decoders, pumps, BIST) qualified on 28 nm and 22FDX U.S. processes lets array-technology teams design only the cell and tile it.
why: Capital and time-to-market: cuts ~18 months and ~$30-50M per new memory entrant, which widens U.S. supply diversity.

title: Fuse-free die: redundancy map lives in the controller
idea: Limit: no fuse banks, antifuse arrays or laser repair on the die. At test, failing rows and columns are recorded in a signed table on the module SPD, and the memory controller remaps addresses before issuing them, with spare rows as ordinary rows.
why: Periphery area (-2-3% of the die), removes laser-repair tools (capital), and allows field repair at boot.

title: Second-harmonic phase sensing reads ferroelectric bits without switching them
idea: Constraint: bits must survive power loss and reads must not wear the cell. Store data as HZO polarization but never switch it to read: a 100 mV, ~1 GHz sinusoid on the plate yields a second-harmonic bitline current whose phase flips with polarization direction (dielectric nonlinearity is odd in P), and a per-column mixer clocked from the same plate tone integrates ~5 ns and latches the sign.
why: Non-volatile with a non-destructive read: no write-back (fact 8), no refresh (fact 3), and read endurance effectively unlimited, since wear happens only on writes.

title: Pyroelectric read: wordline heat pulse makes polarization announce itself
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, and the read must not flip domains. A ~1 ns current pulse through a resistive wordline strap heats one row of ferroelectric capacitors by ~10 K; each cell emits a pyroelectric current whose sign matches its polarization, and charge integrators on the bitlines read it without ever crossing the coercive field.
why: Non-destructive NV read with no reference cells (sign detection). Risk: ns thermal time constants and the ~fJ heating energy per bit.

title: Power-fail dump: every sense amp owns a vertical NV backup string
idea: Constraint: DRAM data must survive power loss without giving up DRAM endurance. Under each SA stripe, a hybrid-bonded layer gives every sense amp its own short FeFET or charge-trap string; on power-fail detect, all banks open rows in lockstep and ~2M SAs per die program their bits in parallel, dumping 32 Gb in ~1 ms from on-package capacitors, then restore through the same SAs at power-up.
why: NV DRAM with no NVDIMM flash controller or battery; backup parallelism ~1000x NVDIMM-N, and the NV layer sees one write per power cycle, so its endurance is irrelevant.

title: Dirty-row trickle persistence bounds the power-fail energy budget
idea: Constraint: survive sudden power loss with only a tiny hold-up capacitor. Periphery keeps one dirty bit per row and an in-die copy engine uses idle refresh slots to copy dirty rows into an on-die NV bank, capping outstanding dirty rows at N (e.g., 4k), so hold-up energy covers just N rows.
why: Backup energy and capacitor size drop 100-1000x compared with a full-die dump; the copy reuses refresh bandwidth that is spent anyway (fact 3).

title: Normally-on wordline clamps turn IGZO DRAM non-volatile for months
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, using a capacitor cell. Oxide-semiconductor (IGZO) access transistors leak ~1e-20 A, so the only threat when power drops is wordlines floating up. Each wordline gets a depletion-mode IGZO pull-down held off by the live supply; when power vanishes it turns on by itself and clamps every wordline to ground, giving months of unpowered retention.
why: NV with DRAM endurance and speed, no ferroelectric wear, and a periphery cost of one tiny device per wordline driver; refresh shrinks to a power-up scrub (fact 3).

title: Dual-mode HZO: linear dielectric daily, ferroelectric only at shutdown
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, without ferroelectric fatigue. The capacitor runs as a sub-coercive high-k DRAM cell during operation; at power-fail, bipolar plate-line drivers pulse +/-Vc row by row so each cell's stored charge sets its polarization, and at power-up a destructive ferroelectric read with a dual-reference SA reloads the charge state.
why: NV plus unlimited daily endurance, since the ferroelectric switches once per power cycle; HZO's k (~30-40) also eases the capacitor wall (fact 1).

title: Charge-trap access transistor captures each cell's bit at shutdown
idea: Constraint: non-volatile with zero added cell area. The access transistor's gate stack includes a nitride trap layer; at power-fail, bitlines float and a high wordline pulse lets each storage node's own potential (0 or 1 V) set the drain-edge field, injecting charge asymmetrically; at power-up SAs sense the Vt shift by reverse-reading through a gate ramp, then rewrite the capacitors.
why: Per-cell NV backup in the existing footprint (no backup layer). Risk: write disturb and program margin from a 1 V difference.

title: Hadamard-coded multi-row reads give tiny MRAM signals root-N SNR
idea: Constraint: non-volatile resistive cells with weak signal. Because MRAM reads are non-destructive, activate N rows at once with +/-1 Hadamard-coded read biases over N sense cycles and invert the code in a small digital block; the Fellgett multiplex advantage gives a sqrt(N) SNR gain per cell (4x at N=16).
why: MRAM sensing margin (low TMR) drives large SAs and references; sqrt(N) lets read current fall 4x (less read disturb) or the SA shrink, and it tolerates lower-TMR, cheaper stacks.

title: Pulse-width-weighted reads: one integrator resolves four NV bits
idea: Constraint: non-volatile cells with ON/OFF ratio above 50x (ReRAM/FTJ). Four cells on one bitline are read at once with wordline pulse widths of 1:2:4:8, so their currents integrate on one capacitor as a binary-weighted charge, and a 4-bit SAR converter returns all four bits.
why: Periphery (fact 7): sense-amp count and read energy per bit fall ~4x; the read is non-destructive so it needs no restore.

title: Normally-off banks: domain-wall latches keep decoder and row state
idea: Constraint: nothing may be lost at power-off, periphery included. Mode registers, open-row addresses and decoder latches use magnetic domain-wall or FeFET latches, so a bank with an NV array power-gates completely between bursts and wakes in ~ns with no re-init or retraining.
why: Idle power: refresh (16-33% of idle) and periphery leakage go to ~0, a big gain for bursty AI-inference memory.

title: Spin-orbit voltage readout: nanomagnets drive inverters, no sense amps
idea: Constraint: non-volatile magnetic bits. Instead of current-mode TMR sensing, pass a small supply current through the bit's spin-injection layer into a strong spin-orbit layer (Bi2Se3/Pt), where the inverse Edelstein/spin-Hall effect converts spin to a charge voltage whose sign follows magnetization (MESO-style); that voltage gates a local inverter directly, with no reference or SA.
why: Periphery (fact 7): deletes SAs and references. Risk: ~10-100 mV output and spin-to-charge efficiency.

title: Bitlines as last-gasp battery for finishing in-flight NV writes
idea: Constraint: no write may be torn when power dies. At power-fail detect, switches tie every precharged bitline and VPP-node capacitance on the die (~3 uF total at 0.5-3 V) to a shared rail that powers completion of in-flight NV writes and a write-buffer flush.
why: Gives ~0.5-1 uJ, enough for ~0.5 MB of MRAM writes, from capacitance already on the die, removing NVDIMM supercaps and external hold-up.

title: In-sense-amp capacitor taps shield finite-endurance NV cells from writes
idea: Constraint: NV cells (FeRAM/MRAM, ~1e10-1e12 cycles) must still behave with DRAM-class endurance. Each sense amp gets four capacitor taps that act as an in-SA DRAM row cache; writes coalesce there, and a row is written to the NV array only on eviction or at power-fail, flushed with an on-die energy reserve.
why: Turns 1e10-cycle NV cells into effectively unlimited-endurance memory for hot rows, at <5% SA-stripe overhead.

title: Switching-time sensing: read FeRAM by when the current peaks
idea: Constraint: non-volatile 1T1C ferroelectric cells shrunk until switching charge is tiny. Sense the time of the current spike rather than its charge: a peak detector plus time-to-digital converter on each bitline tells a switching cell (delayed nucleation peak) from a non-switching one (immediate displacement only), with no reference cell.
why: Immune to capacitor-area variation and fatigue-induced charge loss, so 3D FeRAM cells can shrink until switching charge is ~1 fC; no reference columns (periphery -5%).

title: Antiferroelectric avalanche preamp multiplies femtocoulomb ferroelectric signals
idea: Constraint: non-volatile ferroelectric cells too small to give usable charge. At each SA input, a tiny antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor is biased just below its AFE-to-FE transition field; the cell's switching charge tips it over, releasing a large field-induced polarization step (~5-10x charge gain), and it relaxes back when the bias is removed.
why: Density: lets 3D-stacked FeRAM cells shrink to ~30 nm with ~1 fC signals, with charge gain built from the same HZO/ZrO2 toolset.

title: Persistence-domain DRAM standard: mandatory per-die power-fail dump pin
idea: Constraint: data survives power loss in every server, by standard. Propose a JEDEC/OCP 'DDR-P' profile in which each die has a power-fail pin, an energy-budget register and an in-die backup engine, so hosts can drop batteries, NVDIMM-N modules and flash-backed caches; seed it via U.S. federal procurement of persistent memory.
why: Strategy: creates a market for NV periphery IP in which U.S. firms can lead, and removes ~$50-100 of backup hardware per server.

title: Ferroelectric-imbalanced sense latches keep open rows across power loss
idea: Constraint: open pages must survive an instant power cut with zero dump time. Two small HZO capacitors on each SA's internal nodes are polarized by the latched value in a ~10 ns pulse on power-fail detect (not on every activation, to spare endurance); when power returns, their remanent imbalance biases the latch so it re-resolves to the same value, recovering ~256 kB of open-row state.
why: Zero-latency persistence for in-flight rows (nvSRAM idea at row-buffer scale); complements a slower full-array backup.

title: VCMA-gated shared spin-orbit write lines: one driver per row
idea: Constraint: non-volatile SOT-MRAM, whose large write drivers swell periphery. Run one heavy-metal SOT current line under an entire row of MTJs and select which bits switch with voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy on each MTJ's top electrode, so a single row driver plus low-current column voltage gates replace per-column write drivers.
why: Periphery area: write-driver silicon -70-80%; SOT keeps read and write paths separate, which gives reads effectively unlimited endurance.

title: Read the cell's EMF: electrochemical bits sensed by voltage
idea: Constraint: non-volatile with zero read current. Store bits as ion concentration in a nanoscale electrochemical (ECRAM-like) cell whose open-circuit voltage differs by ~100 mV between states; the SA samples that voltage onto a precharged floating bitline through a high-impedance gate, so the read draws no state-changing current.
why: Read disturb and read energy fall to ~0 (voltage, not current); non-destructive. Risk: ns-speed bitline charging from a high-impedance source.

title: Microwatt refresh island: coin cell keeps IGZO memory alive for years
idea: Constraint: data survives mains loss, with no NV material. Pair hour-retention IGZO DRAM with a tiny always-on periphery island (a ~2 uW clock, counter and row walker) that refreshes one row every ~1 ms from a 20 mAh lithium cell or harvested trickle, while all other periphery is cut off.
why: Quasi-NV with full DRAM endurance and speed; a 32 Gb die needs only ~0.4 uW of refresh, so the cell lasts ~2 years without ferroelectric wear or backup dumps.

title: BEOL oxide-TFT sense amps above NV crossbar: die equals array
idea: Constraint: NV crossbar cells (BEOL-compatible MRAM/ReRAM/FTJ). Build the sense amps, column muxes and local drivers from complementary oxide TFTs (n-IGZO plus p-SnO or Te) in the BEOL directly above or between crossbar tiers, so the front-end silicon under the array holds only global logic.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): die area per bit approaches the array area (~2x density); BEOL processing at <=400 C suits U.S. legacy fabs.

title: Delete plate-line drivers: bitline-only bipolar FeRAM drive
idea: Constraint: non-volatile 1T1C ferroelectric, without FeRAM's large, slow plate-line drivers. Tie all plates to a fixed mid-rail and switch polarization by driving the bitline to +V or -V around it (bipolar bitline drivers built into the SA), so the plate needs no driver and no decoding.
why: Periphery area -8-12% and ~2x faster cycles (plate RC was the bottleneck); plate energy disappears.

title: Lazy restore after power-up: rows restored on first touch
idea: Constraint: data survives power loss via a backup layer, but boot restore must not take milliseconds. A per-row 'restored' bitmap in the periphery, cleared at power-up, lets the memory accept requests immediately; the first touch of a row triggers its restore from the backup layer through the SAs, while a background walker finishes the rest.
why: Instant availability (us instead of ms to s of restore), so NV-backed DRAM suits fast-failover servers and edge devices.
